claim: In July 1994 the torn-apart comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 hit Jupiter; for the first time NASA had spacecraft in place to watch two solar system bodies collide.

beats.caption: A COMET VS JUPITER
beats.vo: A comet was torn into a line of pieces, all aimed at Jupiter.

beats.caption: RIPPED APART
beats.vo: In July 1992 it flew so close that Jupiter's gravity ripped it apart.

beats.caption: A FREIGHT TRAIN OF COMET
beats.vo: Astronomers found it in 1993: more than twenty pieces, labeled A through W, like a freight train.

beats.caption: FIRST TIME EVER WATCHED
beats.vo: From July 16 to 22, 1994, the pieces hit. For the first time, NASA had spacecraft in place to watch two bodies in the solar system collide.

beats.caption: 300 MILLION ATOMIC BOMBS
beats.vo: The blasts threw plumes up to 3,000 kilometers high, with the force of 300 million atomic bombs.

beats.caption: THE SCARS FADED
beats.vo: Jupiter's winds erased the scars. But the dust let scientists track its high-altitude winds for the first time.

credits: Artist's reenactment: stylized, not to scale.
